readerTitle: Three products, one device: how Apple explained the iPhone
caseNote: 실제 기업 사례 (Apple, 2007년 1월 Macworld 키노트) + 가상 적용 (B2B 물류 컨설팅, 가정 관리 서비스)
insight: 완전히 새로운 것을 설명할 때는 기능을 늘어놓지 말고, 청중이 이미 아는 것 몇 개에서 출발해 하나로 묶어 보여준다.
misconception: 새로운 제품일수록 새 이름과 모든 기능을 자세히 알려야 청중이 그 가치를 이해한다.

sources.text: Apple Macworld San Francisco 2007 keynote, January 9, 2007 (공개 영상: 세 제품 소개 방식, 기존 스마트폰 비교 슬라이드)
Apple press release, "Apple Reinvents the Phone with iPhone" (January 9, 2007)
Vogelstein, F. (2013). "And Then Steve Said, 'Let There Be an iPhone'." The New York Times Magazine (시연용 시제품의 불안정성, 정해진 시연 순서)

factChecks.note: 키노트 날짜(2007년 1월 9일)와 장소(샌프란시스코 Macworld)를 Apple 보도자료로 다시 확인하세요.

인용문 "These are not three separate devices, this is one device, and we are calling it iPhone"과 세 제품 이름(widescreen iPod with touch controls, revolutionary mobile phone, breakthrough Internet communications device)을 키노트 영상 원문과 대조하세요. 카드에는 짧게 옮겼습니다.
시제품이 불안정했고 엔지니어들이 정해진 순서로만 시연하도록 준비했다는 내용은 Vogelstein(2013) 보도에 근거합니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다.
미국 출시일(2007년 6월 29일)을 Apple 보도자료로 확인하세요. 소스 URL 두 개가 현재도 유효한지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Three products, one device: how Apple explained the iPhone
body: January 2007, San Francisco. Steve Jobs walked on stage to introduce a phone with almost no buttons, a touchscreen and a full web browser.
Most people in the room had never seen anything like it. Within a few minutes, they understood it. How he did that is a lesson in explaining anything new.

image.label: A presenter on a dark stage with a large blank screen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 어두운 무대 위 발표자 실루엣과 뒤의 큰 스크린. 객석은 앞쪽으로 기울어 집중한 모습. 실제 인물 얼굴, Apple 로고, 실제 제품 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How do you open?
body: You have a device unlike anything your audience owns. It plays music, makes calls and browses the web, all on a touchscreen.
You have a few minutes before people decide what it is. How do you start?

options.text: Walk through every feature and spec so nothing is missed
options.feedback: You'd be complete and accurate. But a long list asks the audience to build the big picture themselves, and most won't.

options.text: Give it a bold new category name and explain that category
options.feedback: A new label feels fresh, but it means nothing yet. You'd spend your few minutes teaching a word instead of the idea.

options.text: Start with things people already know, then show they're one device
options.feedback: You borrow understanding the audience already has. The surprise comes from joining familiar pieces, not from decoding something strange.

cards.title: He announced three products.
body: Jobs said Apple was introducing three things: a widescreen iPod with touch controls, a revolutionary mobile phone, and a breakthrough internet communications device.

He repeated the three names as icons cycled on the screen behind him. The audience began to catch on. Then came the line: these are not three separate devices, this is **one device**, and we are calling it iPhone.
Every listener knew an iPod, a phone and the internet. He only had to add one idea: together.

image.label: Three simple icons merging into one shape
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 음악 노트, 전화 수화기, 지구본 아이콘 세 개가 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 이동하며 하나의 둥근 사각형으로 합쳐짐. 실제 제품 모양이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Anchor the new in the familiar
body: **Anchoring in the familiar** means explaining something new through things your listener already understands, then showing what's different.

People can't absorb many new ideas at once. Each unfamiliar term costs attention. Familiar pieces cost almost nothing, so the listener's attention goes to the one new idea you actually want them to remember.
The new idea in 2007 wasn't music or calls. It was having them in one device.

cards.title: The keynote followed a simple order.
body: Each step did one job:
list: **Start known:** three products the audience already used
**Repeat:** the same three names, until people started saying them too
**Contrast:** a slide of the smartphones of the day, with small fixed keyboards
**Then show:** a live demo only after the idea had landed
cards.callout: The demo proved the message. It didn't have to explain it.

cards.title: It works for a service, too.
body: A logistics consultancy launches a new offer. The first draft of the pitch says: "an integrated supply-chain resilience program." Clients nod and forget it.

The second draft says: "It's your freight audit, your backup supplier list and your staff drill, run as one plan." Each piece is something clients already buy or understand. The new part is that they're joined.
Same offer. The second version takes seconds to grasp.

cards.title: A clear message raises the bar.
body: The phones on stage were reportedly far from finished. Engineers prepared a fixed sequence of steps for the demo, because other paths could crash it. The iPhone didn't go on sale until late June.
Clear framing makes people believe you. If what you deliver doesn't match the story, that clarity turns against you.
Familiar framing can also hide what's truly new. Name the known pieces, but make sure the new part gets said out loud.

cards.title: Now it's a home-services business.
body: You run a cleaning and handyman company. You're launching a yearly plan: a seasonal deep clean, a gutter check and small repairs, booked automatically.
You're texting existing customers about it. Which first line works best?

options.text: "HomeCare 360: total home wellness, all year round."
options.feedback: It sounds polished, but customers have to guess what's inside. A new name only works once people know what it stands for.

options.text: "Your spring clean, your gutter check and your odd-job visit, booked once a year."
options.feedback: Every piece is something they already buy. The new part, booking it all at once, is the only thing they have to learn.

options.text: "Our plan includes 14 tasks across four seasonal visits. Full list below."
options.feedback: Honest and complete, which helps customers who are already interested. But a list rarely makes someone interested in the first place.

cards.title: Explain the new with what people already know.
body: Start from familiar pieces, repeat them, then show the one thing that's different. Save the details and the demo for after the idea lands.
**Try it today:** take something new you're pitching. Describe it in one sentence using only things your listener already buys or uses.
